overview: Kaarta was a Bamana kingdom in western Mali, governed by the Massassi dynasty and often competing with Ségou. Family alliances, farming and warfare helped build its power. The imported map begins in 1783, long after its origins, and shows an unusually broad outline; neither its borders nor its 1878 endpoint precisely describe the independent kingdom.

periods.title: Origins remembered in oral traditions
periods.summary: Stories of the Massassi founders link agricultural households, marriage alliances and expanding political power.

periods.title: A resurgent Bamana kingdom
periods.summary: Kaarta recovered from defeat and became a major regional competitor.

periods.title: Umarian Kaarta
periods.summary: Umar Tal’s forces captured Nioro in 1855. The region then continued under Umarian rule, with resistance and internal struggles.

items.text: A foundation tradition remembers Massa as a successful farmer who married daughters to men willing to join his household and support him. This is a story about how followers and alliances were assembled, rather than a securely dated census of one enormous family.

Kaarta’s ruling clan kept close control over provincial governors and military commanders. Members and allies shared allegiance to its guardian spirit. Politics involved religious obligations and kinship as well as armed force; a ruler needed organized supporters, not merely a grand title.

The royal economy drew on tribute, trade tolls and warfare. Captives could be forced into armies or sold, while women were taken into ruling households. Remembering these people matters: royal expansion could mean the destruction of someone else’s home and freedom.

At Moonia, in territory controlled by Kaarta, Gray’s party received couscous, milk and honey. Their host also supplied fresh water and lodging. A traveler’s special welcome does not describe every family’s dinner, but it gives us an actual meal rather than an invented royal menu.

At Kirrijou, a Khasso town under Kaartan power, Gray recorded grain, rice, groundnuts, onions, livestock and dairy foods. He also complained about shallow wells beside stagnant water. Abundant farmland and reliable drinking water were separate problems for households to solve.

Near Asamangatary, Gray described women making earthenware on a plain also known for rice and onions. Pots required skilled hands as much as fields did. His account places this district at the beginning of what he called Kaarta proper.

sections.title: A visit in 1864, after the conquest

items.text: At Kouroundingkoto in February 1864, Mage heard weaving looms working outdoors. Nearby plains had cotton fields, and women and children gathered around the visitors. This glimpse connects growing a fiber, making cloth and village social life in the same small landscape.

A local religious teacher gave Mage a young goat. It accompanied the expedition and repeatedly stole couscous from village women, to the delight of the traveling party. Apparently a nineteenth-century goat could also mistake everybody else’s dinner for its own invitation.

After Dindanco, Mage met traders bringing slabs of rock salt from Nioro. He described blocks roughly 60 centimeters long and 40 centimeters wide. Salt reached households through several stages of exchange: much more work than shaking a little onto dinner.

Park reported that Kaarta’s ruler issued an Arabic proclamation on a thin wooden board during the 1796 war with Ségou. Elders then explained it aloud. Written messages and spoken explanation worked together; Park did not preserve the original Arabic wording.

A modern Bambara sample is “I ni sogoma!”: “Good morning!” Stephanie Tolk records it in a 2021 account of her Peace Corps service in Mali from 1998 to 2000. This is an attested modern greeting, not a transcription of Kaarta’s lost proclamation.

Umar Tal entered Nioro on 11 April 1855. His forces imposed a new Islamic political order, but conquest did not immediately end resistance. Kaarta remained important to later Umarian states, connecting western recruiting areas with territories farther east.

ending.text: The independent Massassi kingdom fell to Umar Tal in 1855. The name Kaarta continued for the region and its Umarian successor administration; an imported map extending to 1878 must not suggest that the old dynasty still ruled throughout that interval.
